content: Rhinitis is a complex and diverse condition that is often underestimated in its impact. It is a widespread global disease that can significantly affect the quality of life of those who suffer from it. Rhinitis is defined by the presence of one or more nasal symptoms, including sneezing, nasal itching, rhinorrhea (both anterior and posterior), and nasal congestion. The degree of nasal inflammation can vary among individuals. In the United States alone, rhinitis accounts for approximately $9 billion in direct healthcare expenditures annually. Chronic rhinitis is one of the most common conditions encountered by physicians, with allergic rhinitis being the most prevalent subtype. The global prevalence of allergic rhinitis has been steadily increasing, particularly in industrialized nations. Despite its high prevalence, rhinitis is frequently overlooked, underdiagnosed, and inadequately treated. A better understanding of the causes and treatment options for different types of rhinitis could improve patient care and enhance the quality of life for those affected. Historically, rhinitis has been recognized since ancient times. Seasonal allergic rhinitis, commonly known as hay fever, became more prevalent with the industrialization of Western countries in the 19th century. By the late 19th century, it was a common condition in Europe and North America. Nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilic syndrome (NARES) was first described in 1981 by Jacobs et al. Primary atrophic rhinitis has been documented since ancient times by civilizations such as the Egyptians, Greeks, and Indians, and it was formally described by Bernhard Fraenkel in 1876. Rhinitis can be broadly classified into allergic and nonallergic types. Some forms of rhinitis do not fit neatly into either category, and there is often an overlap between allergic and nonallergic rhinitis, referred to as mixed rhinitis. The classification and diagnosis of nonallergic rhinitis are particularly challenging due to its diverse causes and limited understanding compared to allergic rhinitis. Allergic rhinitis is a multifactorial disease influenced by genetic and environmental factors. Aeroallergens, such as dust mite fecal particles, cockroach residues, animal dander, molds, and pollens, trigger allergic responses in the nasal tissue. These allergens elicit IgE-mediated immune responses, leading to varying degrees of nasal inflammation. Nonallergic rhinitis, on the other hand, encompasses a heterogeneous group of poorly understood conditions that require further research and phenotyping. Chronic rhinitis is a common condition seen by physicians, and identifying its underlying cause is essential for effective management. Allergic rhinitis is triggered by inhalation of indoor and outdoor aeroallergens, such as pollens, molds, and animal dander. Nonallergic rhinitis, however, is induced by nonspecific triggers, including chemical odors, cigarette smoke, spicy foods, exercise, and cold air. It is crucial to differentiate rhinitis from other conditions that mimic its symptoms, such as intranasal foreign bodies, cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea, nasal polyps, and tumors. Rhinitis is a highly prevalent global disease. Allergic rhinitis affects an estimated 9–42% of the population, with 10–30% of adults and up to 40% of children experiencing symptoms. Its prevalence has been increasing worldwide, likely due to factors such as rising airborne pollution, increased dust mite populations in poorly ventilated environments, and sedentary lifestyles. Over the past 50 years, the prevalence of allergic rhinitis has doubled in some countries, with over 50% of adolescents in certain regions reporting symptoms. Mixed rhinitis is estimated to affect approximately 26 million individuals in the United States. Risk factors for allergic rhinitis include a history of other atopic diseases, such as asthma and atopic dermatitis, as well as a family history of rhinitis. Risk factors for infectious rhinitis include young age, daycare attendance, and exposure to air pollutants. Allergic rhinitis rarely occurs in isolation and is often associated with other atopic conditions, such as eczema, asthma, and allergic eye disease (allergic rhinoconjunctivitis). Most individuals with asthma also have rhinitis, and allergic eye disease is reported in nearly all patients with allergic rhinitis. Nonallergic rhinitis is also linked to asthma. Rhinitis, particularly infectious rhinitis, frequently extends into the sinuses, leading to rhinosinusitis. Children with nonallergic rhinitis are more likely to experience remission compared to those with allergic rhinitis, which tends to persist. Remission occurs in up to 73% of four-year-old children with nonallergic rhinitis by the age of eight. Rhinitis is a significant cause of lost school and workdays and imposes a substantial financial burden on society. Untreated or poorly managed chronic rhinitis is associated with reduced quality of life, disordered sleep, impaired work performance, and various comorbidities. A thorough history of rhinitis symptoms is essential, including identifying the most bothersome symptoms, symptom patterns, precipitating factors, environmental history, coexisting conditions, family history, and previous responses to medications. A detailed physical examination is critical for accurate diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of complications associated with chronic rhinitis. All potentially affected organ systems should be examined, with particular attention to the upper respiratory tract. Allergic rhinitis can be confirmed by detecting specific IgE reactivity to relevant aeroallergens through skin testing (skin-prick or intradermal tests) or serum-specific IgE testing, such as the radioallergosorbent test (RAST). Chest X-rays are generally not clinically relevant for diagnosing rhinitis unless needed to evaluate associated comorbid conditions. Similarly, CT scans are not routinely required but may be indicated for complicated rhinosinusitis or suspected pathological conditions, such as atrophic rhinitis. Nasal endoscopy is a valuable diagnostic tool for identifying sinonasal pathologies and anatomical variations that are not visible on anterior rhinoscopy. It should be considered early in the diagnostic process to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of the nose and sinuses. The choice of medical therapy for rhinitis depends on its cause and severity. Commonly used medications include antihistamines and corticosteroids. Avoiding triggers and using saline nasal irrigation can also provide significant benefits. Allergen-specific immunotherapy is recommended for appropriately selected patients with allergic rhinitis. Surgery is rarely required for managing rhinitis. However, surgical intervention may be necessary for structural or mechanical problems or coexisting comorbid conditions.
